en: Ātreyatilaka (The Characteristics of the Reflection).
Homage to the Buddha!
In the *Ātreyatilaka*, a Buddhist treatise, as well as in other ancient works,
the characteristics for measuring a statue have been stated by the sages of old. (1)
Having gathered those [elements] here into one and having formed them into a single mass in their proper order,
and having bowed to the omniscient Lord, the characteristics of the image (arcā) are now described.

A tāla consists of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas), as does a vitasti; the face itself is likewise [measured]. This is to be known as the measure for an image (arcā); a golaka is two finger-breadths, and a kalā is one [finger-breadth].
A fourth part of a leaf is known as a measuring finger (māpanāṅgulikā);
from that, a wise man should understand a barleycorn (yava) to be one-eighth of a finger.
It is traditionally taught that this is for the purpose of determining the limbs and minor members of the image;
by this very procedure, the wise man should measure the statue.
Having divided the entire extent of the form-body into nine parts,
one should make the face one *tāla* in height and likewise in width.
That which has the shape of the letter *va*, the luster of a mango, and the appearance of a bird's egg or a sesame seed,
yet is deficient by half a finger-breadth, is desired as being of the form of the letter *va*.
With a reduction of two finger-breadths, the face becomes like a mango;
with a reduction of two and a half finger-breadths, it is said to have the shape of a bird's egg.
One should avoid a space of three finger-breadths for the name-mark shaped like a sesame seed;
one should likewise avoid it on the cheeks of all four faces.
The face of women is desired to have the shape of a sesame seed;
by fashioning the face contrary to the scriptures, the sacrificer perishes.
Having placed the scripture at its head, it prospers together with its kinsmen;
likewise, having brought forth the arrival of the scriptures, the wise man should cause the worship of the images to be performed. ||11||
One should fashion the second sphere and the head portion in the shape of an umbrella;
the forehead is declared to be half a finger and two spheres in height. ||12||
The forehead is fixed at five *golaka*s in width;
the length of the nose is said to be two *kala*s and two *yava*s. (13)
The width at the top is two *yavas*; the projection (*niṣkāsa*) is one and a half *aṅgulas*;
above, on both sides, it is two *aṅgulas*, and the nose (*nāsā*) is three *yavas* thick.

At the base of the bamboo, which is circular and equal to half a finger-breadth, there should be two barley-corns; the two channels should be three barley-corns wide and beautifully shaped like conch shells. (15)
Thus, the tongue-ball joined with the mind is praised;
it has the appearance of a sesame flower and resembles the beak of a parrot. (16)
Its lower part is said to be three finger-breadths and two barley-corns;
one should make the upper lip six barley-corns and the upper lip [itself] four barley-corns.
The *gojī* (fillet) situated above it should be made three-eighths of a finger in width;
the lower *bhojaka* (fillet) should be equal to it, with a width of two fingers. ||18||

One should fashion the lower lip with six barley-corns in thickness at its center and adorned with various lines; the upper lip should be made half a finger-breadth thick and slightly recessed. ||19||
The chin is two finger-breadths in transverse width and ten barley-corns in length;
the space between the eyebrows is half a finger-breadth, and their length should be five finger-breadths. ||20||
The brow-line, measuring half a barley-corn, is unbroken and shaped like a bow;
the eye is two fingers long, with two barley-corns added from one-third [of that length]. (21)
The three parts of the pupil (locana) are likewise proclaimed to be the white star (tāra);
one should make its three parts black, as is fully proclaimed.
The two corners of the eyes should be known as resembling the petals of the kumuda and utpala lotuses, like the belly of a fish; the space between them is two finger-breadths. (23)
The two ears should be two finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in length;
the projection of the ear at the back is proclaimed to be two finger-breadths.
The *tuṭikā* should be two finger-breadths in length, and its width should be half of that;
the width of the ear-ornament (*karṇavartī*) should be one-fourth of a finger-breadth.
The secret part [of the ear] consists of two or three *yava*s; the *pāśikā* should be made according to its beauty.
The configuration at the base of the *karttarī* is proclaimed as the *karṇanāla*. ||26||
Between both ears, the head measures eighteen finger-breadths;
the back of the forehead is fourteen finger-breadths—of this there is no doubt. (27)
The space between the eyebrows and the eyes is proclaimed to be the *golaka*;
the middle distance from the chin to the root of the ear shall be eight finger-breadths.
Likewise, the chin and the forehead should be made equal to the eyes;
one should measure the corners of the mouth and the pupils on both sides using a straight line. (29)
One should strike the line of the eyebrows and the top of the ear with a straight thread;
likewise, one should strike the bridge of the nose and the middle of the eye with equal precision. (30)
The protrusion from the mouth is two *golakas*, and the length of the neck is likewise;
from the base of the shoulders to the root of the ears, it should be three *golakas*.
Below the chin, one should fashion a fleshy protuberance (māṃsavartula) as is aesthetically pleasing;
then, according to the measurement of its length, one should shorten the neck of the female figure. 32.
Then there is the original matted-hair arrangement and curly locks of hair;
likewise, the crown, the three-pronged crest, and the broken diadem.
Their length should be made eight finger-breadths, and not more than that. I shall now describe the auspicious or inauspicious dimensions of the mouth-opening (mukhadvāra). ||34||
One should make a slight smile imbued with a trace of sweetness;
one should avoid from afar a face that is astringent, pungent, angry, sour, bitter, or distorted by pain. (35)
Hereafter, I shall explain the measurement and characteristics of bodies:
a wise person should fashion two openings from the region of the heart down to the navel. (36)
The root of the penis from all sides, the two lateral flanks, the buttocks, the space between the heart and the nipples, and the interval between the nipples [are the locations for piercing]. (37)
From the side of the neck to the shoulder-head is proclaimed to be one tāla;
the distance between the navel and the nipple is fourteen aṅgulas. (38)
The line for the neck (samamūtra) should be drawn, as well as the line from the neck to the tip of the shoulder;
the width between the two shoulders is declared to be three tālas. ||39||
One should make the back [of the breast] six finger-breadths wide, and likewise the space from the armpit to the edge of the breast;
the circle at the side of the nipple should be the size of one *golaka*. 40.
The nipples should be circular and two yavas in size; the navel-circle should be three yavas in size, and the navel itself should be made deep and marked by a clockwise curl. 41.
The two testicles should be three finger-breadths [in length], while the penis should be four finger-breadths;
the buttocks, rising eight finger-breadths above [the anus], should be plump, round, and very beautiful.
Those who know the truth praise the length of the arms as being four times that of the face;
the upper arms (bāhu) should be eight kalās long, and the forearms (prabāhu) nine golakas.
The middle finger should form a single sphere (golaka) with a length equal to the palm;
the thumb should form two spheres, and the little finger should be equal to that [thumb]. 44.
The ring finger is to be known as shorter than the middle finger by half a nail;
the index finger is to be known as shorter than the middle finger by one full nail. 45.
One should fashion the width of the thumb as nine barleycorns,
and for the middle finger, one should apply a width of eight and a half barleycorns across.
Both [the middle and ring fingers] should be made eight barley-corns [in length], while the little finger is seven barley-corns;
the binding of the jewel from the base of the little finger is considered to be five finger-breadths [in width]. 47.
One should know its measurement by the width of the palm, from the base of the thumb up to the point where the two spheres of the binding-jewel [end]. 48.
From the base of the thumb to the base of the index finger is one and a half kalās;
each of those fingers should have three joints, while the thumb should have two. (49)
The joints of the thumb and the fingers are prescribed to be equal;
one should employ them so that their tips are well-rounded and slender, and their articulations are well-knit.
A wise person should have his fingernails made half the length of his own finger across, and half a joint in length; at the base, they should be shaped like a crescent moon. 51.
One should make the hand five fingers long and its side two fingers wide;
one should make the palm full and adorned with auspicious lines. 52.
I shall now describe the lines on the hands, which are the auspicious marks of the gods:
the conch, the lotus, the banner, the thunderbolt, the wheel, the svastika, and the earring. (53)
One should likewise fashion a water-pot, a moon, an umbrella, the Śrīvatsa mark, a garment, a trident, a garland of barley, and the earth.
Between the navel and the private parts, one should mark the root of the thighs evenly;
the length of the thighs is two spans, and the shanks are twice as long as the face. ||55||
The two knees should be two *kalās* each; the two ankles are recorded as one *kalā* each; the two heels should be known as two *kalās* each, having the shape of ripe bimba fruits. (56)
The foot is seven finger-breadths wide and ten finger-breadths in length;
the length of the big toe is prescribed to be one-fourth of the foot.
The index finger is equal to that [middle finger]; the middle finger is less by two barley-corns;
and the little finger is less by half the nail of the ring finger, its joint being reduced. 58.
The width of the thumb is recorded as eleven barley-corns;
the distance between the tips of the needle and the thumb should be three barley-corns.
In the definition of measurements, the needle-point (sūcī) is described as being eight and a half barley-corns in width at its middle,
and the ring-finger (anāmā) as being eight barley-corns in width.
The two thumbs are described as being shaped like mango blossoms;
one should place them upon the foot in the form of a tortoise shell. 61.
The toes are described as being shaped like leeches;
the feet should be made level, and the nails are traditionally said to be shaped like oyster shells.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the circumference:
the circumference of the head should be known as thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas). ||63||
The neck has a width of eight finger-breadths and its circumference is three times that;
the width between the two armpits here is twenty finger-breadths.
The wise one should make it nineteen digits in circumference;
the base, middle, and tip of the two arms should be eight, six, and four digits respectively.
The mandala should be three times the measure of its own width;
the width at the center of the belly should be known to be fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas). ||66||
Its lower part is sixteen finger-breadths, and the waist is eighteen finger-breadths;
at the base of the thighs it is six globes, and in the middle of the shanks it is six finger-breadths.
At the end of the shanks, the wise one should know the width to be two units;
for all of these [parts], the mandala should be three times that.
Likewise, where all the fingers possess roundness and the tip emerges from the back [of the hand], that is proclaimed as the single *kalama* mudrā. (69)
One should make the back straight like a bamboo staff, and the buttocks should hang down evenly;
likewise, one should make the thighs, the calves, and the heels hang down evenly. (70)
O twice-born one, one should know this in brief as the characteristic of the *pṛṣṭha*:
the pearl necklace, the girdle, the bracelets, the armlets, and the earrings. (71)
One should also have the arrangement of garments and cloths placed upon the body.
Now, the merits and defects of the images are being stated according to their superiority or inferiority. (72)
One should provide a very stable site endowed with great length and breadth;
the head [of the structure] should be made like an umbrella, which bestows an abundance of wealth and grain. (73)

And on the forehead of one who bestows eternal prosperity, O fair-browed one, there shall be a line; that well-fashioned mark becomes an object of worship, and his progeny is born with happiness. (74)
An image with a shell-like neck always bestows all accomplishments;
a body in the lion-posture increases prosperity and strength. (75)

His two arms are shaped like the trunks of elephants, accomplishing all desires and aims; they constantly bring about an abundance of crops, destroy [misfortune], and create prosperity through good harvests. (76)

An image that has thighs like plantain stalks, increases goats and cattle, thrives in its village, possesses a beautiful pedestal, and has well-proportioned feet, shall be a promoter of virtuous conduct and learning. (77)
Thus the praise of the images has been stated; now he speaks of the defect of being deficient:
"There shall be famine and the ruin of the kingdom if [the image] is deficient in width and length. (78)
If [the bird] is without its body, one becomes hunchbacked; if without its nose, one becomes diseased.
A glance to the left portends the destruction of livestock, while an upward glance signifies the loss of wealth. (79)
One who has small eyes, circular eyes, or squinting eyes, as well as one with a downward gaze or a look that avoids the eyes—such a person one should avoid from afar. (80)
If the image has a sunken belly, there will always be the destruction of crops; if the image lacks broad hips, the fetus will perpetually miscarry. (81)
The nose, the eye, and the finger—these three being short are great defects;
likewise, the shank, the neck, and the chin—these three being long are great defects. (82)
There are three subtle major defects: the head, the ears, and the nose;
there are three gross major defects: the joints, the belly, and likewise the nails.
Three [limbs] that are sunken are great defects: the two hands, the two feet, and the eyes;
three [limbs] that are short are great defects: the neck, the shoulders, and the arms. (84)
Having thus understood the faults and virtues, the wise man should perform the worship;
the characteristics of the nine *tālas*, as well as the length and circumference, have been fully proclaimed. (85)
In the case of a god, the face is certainly eight [tālas];
for a divine being it is eight, and for a human being it is eight tālas; and for the mother, it is seven and eight [tālas]. (86)
The face (the beautiful one) is declared to be equal in circumference to its height, measuring seventy-six tālas.
And this [definition] has been formulated according to the rule by Maitreya. ||87||
Having made the length eight faces, the wise one [should determine] the characteristics of the goddesses;
having made the face six kalās, the body eleven kalās. (88)
The neck, the breasts, the two limbs, and the space between the lips and the mouth—
all these are the face of a woman (mūrti).
And the perfected one is ordained for the goddesses as well. ||89||
Having made the middle [of the torso] eight finger-breadths, the hips are recorded as five kalās;
one should make the waist twenty finger-breadths, and the thighs eleven kalās.
The knees should be three finger-breadths [in width], and the mass [of the thigh] twenty finger-breadths;
one should make the ankle two finger-breadths—this is the auspicious characteristic of the goddesses. 91.
Having made a circle of thirty finger-breadths on the head, the root of the arm should be five finger-breadths; the mandala should be three times that. ||92||
The wrist is three finger-breadths [in width], and the circles [of the hands] are likewise;
the circumference at the middle of the thigh is three times six kalās (eighteen finger-breadths). 93.
In the middle, the shank shall be five finger-breadths; the mandala should be three times that.
In all cases, the [measurements] of the fingers should likewise be made threefold. 94.
One should make the side-glance, the breasts, and the hips slightly more prominent, so that there is no distress in her gaze.
It would become space. ||95 ||
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of a goddess according to the eight-tāla system.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the measurement and characteristics of children;
the stature of those who possess the form of children is sixfold, and their generalship is likewise sixfold. (96)
The auspicious characteristics of the images of the Vināyakas and Yakṣas should be known: there is a spherical protuberance (golaka) on the head, and the face consists of six such globes. 97.

One should make the neck two finger-breadths [in width]; it should be twenty finger-breadths in the body. At the navel, there should be a hollow of three finger-breadths, with a curvature of half a golaka. ||98||
One should make the thighs seven kalās and the knees likewise;
one should make the ankle-bone six kalās, and the ankle-joint is traditionally held to be one aṅgula.
The heel is three finger-breadths wide, according to the proper sequence;
the feet are five units long, and from that, the girth of the big toe is established.

One should make the thumb equal in size to a needle; the middle finger should be two barley-corns less; the ring finger should be one joint (or barley-corn) less than a nail; and the little finger should be one barley-corn less. 101.
The distance from the collarbone to the armpit is eight finger-breadths, and the upper arms are nine finger-breadths;
the forearms are five *gola*s, and the length of the hand is two *gola*s.
The middle finger should be two *gola*s; the index finger should be [two *gola*s] minus a nail;
the middle joint of the ring finger should be made [one *gola*] minus a nail; and the ring finger [should be one *gola*] minus a joint (or a barley-corn).
They are inferior when the big toe and the little toe are long. ||103||
Now, therefore, I shall explain in detail the various proportions:
the head should be two and a half kalās, and its circumference three times that. (104)
The middle of the face, as well as the tips of the ears and the nose, should be six *kalās*;
the neck-midpoint should be three *karas*, and the belly should be sixteen *aṅgulas*.
In the middle of the body is the six-golaka [measurement], and the waist is seven golakas;
the middle of the thighs is four golakas, and the knee is two kalas and six yavas.
In the middle, the shank is five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and the ankle is three finger-breadths;
the two feet are proclaimed to be two kalās and two finger-breadths respectively in width.
The space between [the fingers] is recorded as nine barley-corns and a thumb-breadth;
one should make the needle eight barley-corns, and the middle [space] seven barley-corns. (108)
The wise man should fashion the beautiful toes of the foot such that the middle toe is six barley-corns long and the little toe is five barley-corns long. 109.
The heel is likewise proclaimed to be three finger-breadths in width;
the big toe is eight [finger-breadths], and the middle toe is nine and seven [respectively]. (110)
Thus ends the definition of the six forms in the *Ātreyatilaka*.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the ten-tāla [measurement] for Brahmā, the goddess Carcikā, the sages, and the Brahmarākṣasas. (111)
One should have a beautiful image made of the divine Buddhas; the wise man should have images of these made, but never of others. 112.
The head should be two *golaka*s in measure, and the face likewise six *golaka*s;
one should make the neck two *golaka*s, and the body twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Know that the buttocks are two *kalās* in measure; the waist should be five *kalās*.
The thighs are twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*), and the knees are traditionally held to be five finger-breadths each.
The two shanks are six fingers wide, and the two ankles are recorded as being three fingers [in width];
the lower portions should be fashioned well-proportioned at five fingers.
The portions of the upper arms (bāhu) should be made as eight *golakas*, and the forearms (*prabāhu*) should be known by the wise as ten *golakas*. 116.
And let those who contemplate the scriptures understand that the portion of the sprout-like hand consists of six kalās; this should be performed by those engaged in these [practices]. 117.
Thus ends the definition of the ten-beat rhythm (*daśatāla*) in the *Ātreyatilaka*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Saptatāla measure:
the head is to be known as three aṅgulas, and the face is exactly six kalās. (118)
The neck should be known to be three finger-breadths [in width], and one should fashion it with the characteristic spiral of a conch shell;
it should be nineteen finger-breadths [in length], beautifully adorned with the circular marks of a divine being. (119)
The hip is one finger-breadth, and the spherical buttock region is nineteen finger-breadths;
the thigh and the knee are each three finger-breadths. ||120||
The shank is nineteen finger-breadths, the ankle is considered one finger-breadth, and the lower part is three finger-breadths; such is the image of seven tālas. (121)
The [shoulder] should be made eight finger-breadths [in width], and the tips of its shoulders likewise;
the arms are to be known as one *tāla* in measure. 122.
O best of sages, the seven globes (golaka) up to the forearms should be fashioned;
the portion for the sprout-like hands is proclaimed to be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
This is the human proportion that must be executed by those who contemplate the scriptures. 123.
Thus ends the definition of the seven tālas in the Ātreyatilaka.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the four-tāla [measure]:
one should make the head one finger-breadth and the face twelve finger-breadths. (124)
Know that the neck is one finger-breadth; the body is twelve finger-breadths;
the hips are half a finger-breadth, and the waist is considered to be one finger-breadth. 125.
The thigh should be nine finger-breadths; the knee is recorded as one finger-breadth.
The shank is to be known as nine finger-breadths, and the ankle should be half a finger-breadth.
The lower portions should be fashioned, each proclaimed to be one finger-breadth; the hikkā and the tip of its shoulder (aṃsa) should be known as four kalās. 127.
The two arms (bāhu) together with the elbow-joints (trigolaka) are eight finger-breadths;
the forearms (prabāhu) are to be known as seven finger-breadths in height, as is the hand-palms (karapallava). 128.
O best of sages, the flesh-wicks should be prepared according to their beauty; thus has the measurement for the dwarf [wick] been described. 129.
Thus ends the definition of the four-beat measure (*catustāla*) in the *Ātreyatilaka*.
I shall now proclaim the arrangement for the great image; listen!
An image measuring fifteen cubits is known as the smallest.
The middle [size] should be known as double that, while the superior is recorded as triple. Beyond this one should not proceed if one desires one's own welfare. ||131||
Deities that are burnt, decayed, broken, or even cracked—whether they remain as they are or are being restored—will always cause defects. (132)
With a burnt image, there is drought; with a decayed image, loss of wealth;
with a broken image, destruction of the family; one should predict war from a cracked image. (133)
Whether it be an image, a linga, a goddess, or a group of Mothers, one should swiftly uproot them by means of the ritual procedure prescribed by rule. 134.

Having offered flowers, water for honor (arghya), incense, food offerings (naivedya), and even a sacrificial oblation (bali), as well as two garments, he should be engaged in the rite of the fire-oblation (homa). ||135||
One should cause the water for the pacification of the Brahmins to be prepared with Vedic mantras;
likewise, there should be a cord made of wool, one of muñja grass, as well as those of fine silk and linen. (136)
The ritual has been thus prescribed; here, a rope is also enjoined.
Having tied it to the hump of the bull, one should pull out the withered deity.
An image made of stone should be placed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in places with abundant water;
one should likewise deposit it at the confluence of rivers.
One who desires his own welfare should melt all of these—gold, silver, copper, and even that made of bell-metal—with fire. (139)
The image should be made of wood and wrapped in a new cloth;
having anointed it with ghee and honey, one should cause it to be illuminated by fire.
If the image should be made of earth or even of clay,
one should dig into the ground and place it at the level of the head, and then fill it up.
Alternatively, one should quickly install either an image (arcā) or a linga;
endowed with all auspicious characteristics, one should install it according to the prescribed rite. ||142||
It brings welfare to the twice-born, the young, the old, and to human beings;
the king attains victory, and there shall be an increase in crops. ||143||
That noble-souled person who performs the restoration of dilapidated images is honored in the world of the gods for hundreds of thousands of millions of yugas. (144)
The restoration of the *Ātreyatilaka* is completed.
If the image should be made of earth or even of clay, one should dig into the ground and place it up to the head; then, one should fill it [with earth]. (141)
Alternatively, one should quickly install either an image (arcā) or a linga;
endowed with all auspicious characteristics, one should install it according to the prescribed rite. ||142||
And for the welfare of the twice-born, the young, the old, and human beings,
the king shall obtain victory, and there shall be an increase in crops. (143)
The great-souled one who performs the restoration of dilapidated images is honored in the world of the gods for hundreds of thousands of millions of yugas. (144)
The restoration of the *Ātreyatilaka* is completed.
